episodes.text: Three colonies — Veridian-A, B, and C — share a single cargo ledger. A 22-minute light-lag separates them. A blackout severed communication 6 hours ago. Colony A allocated Crate 7700 to a medical convoy. Colony C allocated the same crate to a fuel shipment 4 minutes later. Both believe they acted correctly.
episodes.title: The Severed Connection

episodes.text: How can a system maintain a single truth when its parts can't talk to each other?

episodes.data:
Colony A  <--- x(Blackout)x ---> Colony C
[Crate 7700: Meds]           [Crate 7700: Fuel]

episodes.analogy: Like carving a promise into stone, rather than writing it in sand.
episodes.explanation: The 'D' in ACID. Once the database says 'committed', the data must persist through crashes.
episodes.technical_explanation: Durability means committed data is written to persistent storage and survives system failures — even a crash immediately after commit.
episodes.title: Durability
Ensuring Durability
episodes.context: Complete the transaction to ensure the change is durable.

ROLLBACK.why_wrong: ROLLBACK undoes the transaction instead of saving it.
ROLLBACK.confusing_with: You are confusing saving changes with canceling them.

episodes.explanation: Durability means committed data is written to persistent storage and survives system failures — even a crash immediately after commit.
episodes.question: Which ACID property guarantees that once a transaction is committed, it survives crashes?

Atomicity.why_wrong: Not quite. Atomicity ensures a transaction is all-or-nothing, but it doesn't guarantee the data survives a system failure post-commit.
Atomicity.remember: Check the exact definition of the concept.

Consistency.why_wrong: Not quite. Consistency ensures the database moves from one valid state to another, maintaining defined rules, but doesn't handle crash recovery.
Consistency.remember: Check the exact definition of the concept.

Isolation.why_wrong: Not quite. Isolation ensures concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other, rather than dealing with the persistence of data.
Isolation.remember: Check the exact definition of the concept.

episodes.text: Both colonies committed locally. Neither had stale data when they wrote. Yet the combined ledger is now inconsistent.
episodes.title: The Impossible Triangle

episodes.analogy: Imagine a shared diary. If the network goes down (Partition), you must choose: stop writing in it (sacrifice Availability) to avoid conflicting entries, or let everyone write (sacrifice Consistency) and fix the mess later.
episodes.explanation: You can only have two: Consistency, Availability, or Partition Tolerance.
episodes.technical_explanation: A distributed system can provide at most two of: Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance.
episodes.title: The CAP Theorem
Partition Tolerance Trade-offs
episodes.context: Node B is disconnected from Node A. Node A has strict consistency (CP) enabled. What happens when we query Node A for recently written data that hasn't synced?

returns stale data.why_wrong: With strict consistency, the node prefers to fail rather than return stale data.
returns stale data.confusing_with: You are confusing CP (Consistency/Partition Tolerance) with AP (Availability/Partition Tolerance).

episodes.explanation: The CAP theorem is the fundamental trade-off in distributed database design.
episodes.question: Which theorem states a distributed system cannot simultaneously guarantee Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance?

Amdahl's Law.why_wrong: Not quite. Amdahl's Law describes the theoretical speedup limit of parallel execution, not distributed database consistency.
Amdahl's Law.remember: Check the exact definition of the concept.

The ACID theorem.why_wrong: Not quite. ACID applies to transaction guarantees on a single database node, not distributed partition tolerance.
The ACID theorem.remember: Check the exact definition of the concept.

The BASE theorem.why_wrong: Not quite. BASE is an alternative model to ACID used in NoSQL systems (Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency), not a theorem about hard limitations.
The BASE theorem.remember: Check the exact definition of the concept.

episodes.text: During the blackout, Colony C had no way to know Colony A had already committed. Without coordination, both committed conflicting writes to the same record. Now they are back online, and the system must reconcile.
episodes.title: Reconciliation

episodes.analogy: Like two friends updating a shared grocery list offline and then syncing their phones.
episodes.explanation: Eventual consistency allows temporary divergence but guarantees all nodes will converge to the same state if no new updates arrive.
episodes.technical_explanation: Eventual consistency is used by DynamoDB, Cassandra, and many distributed systems — diverge now, converge later.
episodes.title: Lost Update & Eventual Consistency

episodes.question: If two nodes commit a conflicting update, how should the database decide which one 'wins'?

episodes.explanation: First-writer-wins uses the earliest commit timestamp to determine the authoritative version.
episodes.question: What conflict resolution strategy gives priority to the earliest committed transaction?

Last-writer-wins.why_wrong: Not quite. Last-writer-wins resolves conflicts by keeping the most recently submitted or timestamped data, overwriting earlier commits.
Last-writer-wins.remember: Check the exact definition of the concept.

Manual review.why_wrong: Not quite. Manual review requires human intervention to resolve conflicts, rather than an automated rule based on commit timestamps.
Manual review.remember: Check the exact definition of the concept.

Quorum voting.why_wrong: Not quite. Quorum voting is used to achieve consensus on distributed reads and writes, rather than prioritizing based strictly on the earliest commit time.
Quorum voting.remember: Check the exact definition of the concept.

episodes.text: The Aurelia Array has collected 547 million radio burst records over 12 years. Analysts believe a non-random repeating signal is buried in the noise. The query to find repeating patterns takes 18 seconds. Analysts are giving up before the results arrive.
episodes.title: The Signal in the Noise

episodes.text: Why does querying 547 million rows take so long, and how can we speed it up?

episodes.analogy: Like reading a 1000-page book word-by-word to find a specific character's name.
episodes.explanation: Reading every row in the table from start to finish.
episodes.technical_explanation: A sequential scan reads all blocks of the table in order, regardless of how many rows will match the predicate.
episodes.title: Sequential Scan
Avoiding Sequential Scans
episodes.context: The query is scanning the whole table. Fix the query to allow index usage.
episodes.broken_query: SELECT * FROM signals WHERE event_time::text LIKE '2023%';

change to LIKE '%2023%'.why_wrong: A leading wildcard prevents B-Tree index usage entirely.
change to LIKE '%2023%'.confusing_with: You might be confusing text matching with indexable range queries.
change to LIKE '%2023%'.remember: B-Tree indexes need a known starting point.

episodes.explanation: A sequential scan processes every row — expensive when very few rows match.
episodes.question: What type of scan reads every row in the table from start to finish?

Bitmap scan.why_wrong: Not quite. A bitmap scan builds a bitmap in memory based on an index to fetch rows efficiently, which is different from a naive sequential scan.
Bitmap scan.remember: Check the exact definition of the concept.

Index scan.why_wrong: Not quite. An index scan uses a separate data structure (an index) to quickly find specific rows, rather than reading the entire table sequentially.
Index scan.remember: Check the exact definition of the concept.

Index-only scan.why_wrong: Not quite. An index-only scan retrieves data directly from the index without needing to read the actual table data pages.
Index-only scan.remember: Check the exact definition of the concept.

episodes.text: You propose creating an index on event_time. The planner now estimates it can skip to the relevant time range and read only 1,200 rows instead of 547 million.
episodes.title: Building a Roadmap

episodes.analogy: Like the index at the back of a book, telling you exactly which page to turn to.
episodes.explanation: A self-balancing tree data structure that maintains sorted data and allows rapid searches.
episodes.technical_explanation: A B-tree index is a self-balancing tree where internal nodes guide the search and leaf nodes store (key, row-pointer) pairs in sorted order.
episodes.title: B-Tree Index
Creating an Index
episodes.context: Create a B-Tree index to speed up the time-based query.

TABLE.why_wrong: This command creates an index, not a new table.
TABLE.confusing_with: You are confusing table creation with index creation.
TABLE.remember: CREATE INDEX creates the search structure.

episodes.answer: A balanced tree of sorted key-value pairs
episodes.explanation: A B-tree keeps keys sorted so that range predicates (BETWEEN, >, <) traverse a narrow path rather than the entire dataset.
options: A balanced tree of sorted key-value pairs
episodes.question: What internal data structure does a standard database index typically use?

A bitmap.why_wrong: Not quite. Bitmaps are useful for low-cardinality columns (like boolean values), but standard database indexes typically use B-trees for general-purpose indexing.
A bitmap.remember: Check the exact definition of the concept.

A hash table.why_wrong: Not quite. Hash tables are used for exact match lookups but cannot efficiently support range queries, which are common in databases.
A hash table.remember: Check the exact definition of the concept.

A linked list.why_wrong: Not quite. Linked lists require O(N) traversal time, which is too slow for database indexing where quick lookups are essential.
A linked list.remember: Check the exact definition of the concept.

episodes.text: After adding the time index, analysts add a second filter: frequency_band = 'L'. The planner uses the time index but still scans half the retrieved rows for frequency_band without an index.
episodes.title: Complex Filters

episodes.analogy: Like a phonebook sorted first by Last Name, then by First Name.
episodes.explanation: An index on multiple columns.
episodes.technical_explanation: A composite index stores multiple columns in a single index structure, making it efficient for queries that filter on all indexed columns together.
episodes.title: Composite Index

episodes.context: We need to filter by both event_time and frequency_band.
episodes.query: CREATE INDEX idx_time_band ON signals(event_time, frequency_band);
episodes.question: What type of index covers two or more columns?
steps: Create an index on both columns.
episodes.title: Optimizing with Composite Indexes

Clustered index.why_wrong: Not quite. A clustered index determines the physical sorting order of data in the table, not necessarily the number of columns indexed.
Clustered index.remember: Check the exact definition of the concept.

Covering index.why_wrong: Not quite. A covering index contains all the columns needed for a specific query, which could just be one column or multiple, but 'composite' specifically means multi-column.
Covering index.remember: Check the exact definition of the concept.

Partial index.why_wrong: Not quite. A partial index is built on a subset of a table that satisfies a specific condition, rather than spanning multiple columns.
Partial index.remember: Check the exact definition of the concept.

episodes.text: Despite the composite index, analysts run the pattern-aggregation query hourly and it still takes 3 seconds. The result changes only once every 6 hours but is computed from scratch each time.
episodes.title: The Final Bottleneck

episodes.analogy: Like making a large batch of soup in advance, instead of cooking a fresh bowl every time someone orders.
episodes.explanation: Pre-computing and storing the results of a complex query.
episodes.technical_explanation: A materialized view caches the result on disk and refreshes periodically. OLTP handles high-throughput writes; OLAP handles complex reads. Separating them prevents contention.
episodes.title: Materialized Views & OLAP

episodes.explanation: A materialized view physically stores the query result.
episodes.question: What database object stores the pre-computed result of a query and refreshes it on demand?

A stored procedure.why_wrong: Not quite. A stored procedure is a saved collection of SQL statements that can be executed as a program, not a stored result set.
A stored procedure.remember: Check the exact definition of the concept.

A trigger.why_wrong: Not quite. A trigger is a piece of code that automatically executes in response to certain events on a particular table or view.
A trigger.remember: Check the exact definition of the concept.

A view.why_wrong: Not quite. A standard view is a virtual table that runs its underlying query every time it is accessed, without storing pre-computed results.
A view.remember: Check the exact definition of the concept.

episodes.text: Elias Voss submitted his neural implant for diagnostic review. The archive returns 2 marriages, 2 employers, and 2 sets of childhood memories — each flagged as authentic. The implant stores life-events in a single flat table. Every time Elias moved or changed jobs, someone added a new row. Old rows were never removed. The contradictions multiplied silently.
episodes.title: The Flawed Memory Archive

episodes.text: How do we organize data to prevent contradictions and anomalies when updating records?

episodes.analogy: Like a spreadsheet where you can't cram multiple phone numbers into a single 'Contact Info' box.
episodes.explanation: Every cell must contain a single, indivisible value.
episodes.technical_explanation: 1NF requires atomic values — each cell holds one value, not a comma-separated list or nested set.
episodes.title: First Normal Form (1NF)

episodes.data:
BAD:
| ID | Tags             |
|  1 | work;education   |

GOOD:
| ID | Tag       |
|  1 | work      |
|  1 | education |

episodes.title: Applying 1NF
episodes.context: Fix this schema so it follows 1NF.
episodes.broken_query: CREATE TABLE employees (id INT, skills VARCHAR); -- skills stores 'Java, Python, C++'
options: Create a separate employee_skills table with one skill per row
episodes.answer: Create a separate employee_skills table with one skill per row

Increase VARCHAR length.why_wrong: Increasing the length just allows more comma-separated values, keeping the non-atomic structure.
Increase VARCHAR length.confusing_with: You might be confusing storage limits with logical modeling.
Increase VARCHAR length.remember: 1NF -> atomic values, no lists in a column.

episodes.explanation: 1NF is the foundation: no repeating groups, no multi-valued attributes.
episodes.question: Which normal form requires that every column contain only atomic (indivisible) values?

2NF.why_wrong: Not quite. 2NF requires 1NF and that non-key attributes are fully functionally dependent on the entire primary key.
2NF.remember: Check the exact definition of the concept.

3NF.why_wrong: Not quite. 3NF requires 2NF and that all attributes depend strictly on the primary key, avoiding transitive dependencies.
3NF.remember: Check the exact definition of the concept.

BCNF.why_wrong: Not quite. BCNF is a stricter version of 3NF addressing anomalies in overlapping candidate keys, not basic atomicity.
BCNF.remember: Check the exact definition of the concept.

episodes.text: The implant schema stores person_name and person_city in every event row. Elias's city appears in 312 rows: 309 say 'New Meridian', 3 say 'Old Meridian' — the city he left 14 years ago.
episodes.title: The City Anomaly

episodes.analogy: If your key is (Student ID, Course ID), the Student's Name depends only on Student ID, not Course ID. It should be in a separate table.
episodes.explanation: Every non-key attribute must depend on the whole primary key.
episodes.technical_explanation: A functional dependency X -> Y means knowing X gives you Y. 2NF eliminates partial dependencies.
episodes.title: Functional Dependencies & 2NF

episodes.answer: When the value of one attribute uniquely determines the value of another
episodes.explanation: A functional dependency X → Y means: knowing X's value tells you Y's value with certainty.
options: When two tables share a common column
When the value of one attribute uniquely determines the value of another
When a column cannot be NULL
episodes.question: What is a functional dependency?

When a column cannot be NULL.why_wrong: Not quite. This describes a NOT NULL constraint, ensuring data presence rather than attribute relationships.
When a column cannot be NULL.remember: Check the exact definition of the concept.

When two tables share a common column.why_wrong: Not quite. Sharing a common column often refers to a foreign key relationship for joins, not a functional dependency.
When two tables share a common column.remember: Check the exact definition of the concept.

episodes.text: After 2NF, you split out a people table: (person_id, person_name, employer_id, employer_city). Now employer_city depends on employer_id — not on person_id. The dependency is transitive.
episodes.title: Transitive Chains

episodes.analogy: A table should be about the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.
episodes.explanation: Non-key attributes cannot depend on other non-key attributes.
episodes.technical_explanation: 3NF eliminates transitive dependencies. BCNF strengthens 3NF: for every non-trivial functional dependency X -> Y, X must be a superkey.
episodes.title: Third Normal Form (3NF) & BCNF

episodes.explanation: 3NF requires that every non-key attribute depend directly on the primary key, not via a transitive chain.
episodes.question: What normal form eliminates transitive dependencies — where a non-key column depends on another non-key column?

1NF.why_wrong: Not quite. 1NF ensures all columns have atomic values and each row is unique, but does not address transitive dependencies.
1NF.remember: Check the exact definition of the concept.

2NF.why_wrong: Not quite. 2NF removes partial dependencies on a composite primary key, but does not handle dependencies among non-key columns.
2NF.remember: Check the exact definition of the concept.

4NF.why_wrong: Not quite. 4NF eliminates multi-valued dependencies, going beyond the requirements of eliminating transitive dependencies.
4NF.remember: Check the exact definition of the concept.

episodes.text: After normalizing to BCNF, the memory search must JOIN 6 tables to reconstruct one event record. The planner estimates 14ms per lookup. The implant's real-time interface needs sub-millisecond recall.
episodes.title: The Need for Speed

episodes.analogy: Like printing a summary sheet of the most common facts, so you don't have to search 6 different filing cabinets.
episodes.explanation: Intentionally adding redundancy to speed up reads.
episodes.technical_explanation: Denormalization deliberately combines normalized tables or adds redundant columns to reduce the number of JOINs for frequent read queries.
episodes.title: Denormalization

episodes.question: When is it acceptable to intentionally violate Normal Forms in a production database?

episodes.explanation: Denormalization is the intentional reversal of some normalization steps — trading write anomaly risk for faster reads.
episodes.question: What technique intentionally introduces redundancy to improve read performance at the cost of update complexity?

Indexing.why_wrong: Not quite. Indexing creates a separate data structure for fast lookups, rather than redundantly embedding data across tables.
Indexing.remember: Check the exact definition of the concept.

Normalization.why_wrong: Not quite. Normalization is the process of eliminating redundancy by organizing data into distinct tables.
Normalization.remember: Check the exact definition of the concept.

Partitioning.why_wrong: Not quite. Partitioning divides a large table into smaller, more manageable pieces, rather than introducing duplicate data for reads.
Partitioning.remember: Check the exact definition of the concept.
